content: The Creeping Buttercup (Ranunculus repens) is a flowering plant belonging to the Buttercup family, native to Europe and the Pacific Northwest. It is characterized by its bright yellow flowers and stolons, which are horizontal stems that produce roots and new plants at their nodes. The plant has three-lobed, dark green leaves with white spots that emerge from the nodes. The stems, which also grow from the nodes, are covered in fine hairs. One distinguishing feature of the Creeping Buttercup is its relatively large flowers compared to other buttercup species, although under poor growing conditions, the flowers may be as small as 10 mm in diameter. Additionally, the plant is low-lying and spreads via stolons. Creeping Buttercup, originally native to Europe and the Pacific Northwest, was introduced to various regions worldwide as an ornamental plant. However, it has since become an invasive species in many areas. The plant thrives in fields and pastures, particularly in wet soil conditions. Like most buttercups, Ranunculus repens is toxic, but its toxic properties are neutralized when the plant is dried as hay. The plant has an acrid taste, which deters cattle from consuming it. This avoidance allows the buttercup to exploit the grazed areas around it, spreading further through its stolons. Additionally, the plant can spread through the transportation of contaminated hay. Contact with the sap of the Creeping Buttercup can cause irritation to the skin and mucous membranes.
